A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SUDOLM and the same underlying research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a complete comparison; moved material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original medical and TOFU access-control experiments, general-utility results, and a model-response case study in Table 2 and Figures 3–4.

after.justification: v2 reports original access-control, answer-quality, general-utility, and incorrect-key experiments across three models in Tables 1–3.

M1.justification: The random ten-token system-prompt key, preference-pair construction, authorization-conditioned DPO objectives, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Section 3.2 simplifies the rejected-response explanation without establishing a procedural change.

E1.justification: v2 adds ARC-Challenge to general-utility evaluation and tests privileged queries under randomly guessed incorrect keys. The medical Chat-Doctor and TOFU applications, MMLU, and MT-Bench remain, making this a limited extension of coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds direct Medical SFT and TOFU SFT comparators for privileged-task performance and general utility. The vanilla and Anchor access-control comparators, and the instruction-placement comparator in Figure 3, are retained.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from Llama3-8B-Instruct to include Llama2-7B and 13B, with explicit keyed and unkeyed utility comparisons. New protocols include TOFU ROUGE-L recall, reference-based GPT-4 medical scoring, five-shot ARC-Challenge, and incorrect-key testing at lengths 5, 10, and 20 with ten keys per length. The existing medical split and access-control metric definitions remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 and Table 3 introduce a dedicated robustness analysis asking whether randomly guessed keys unlock privileged answers, across three key lengths, three models, and both applications. The earlier system-versus-user-prompt case study remains Figure 3, relocated to Appendix C.

E5.justification: Neither version reports model-run replication, seeds, dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The ten incorrect keys per length in v2 are sampled evaluation inputs; their average refusal rates do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes Llama3 medical accuracy/recall/F1 from 99.40/99.33/99.50 to 99.80/100/99.83; its TOFU row is unchanged. Tables 1–3 add extensive model, SFT, answer-quality, ARC, and incorrect-key results. Earlier TOFU utility scores of 7.86 MT-Bench and 62.5 MMLU are replaced by keyed scores of 7.55/61.5 and unkeyed scores of 7.52/61.3; v1 did not identify its key condition.

T1.justification: The substantive knowledge partition, authorization rule, DPO formulation, and combined training objective are retained. Removing parenthetical query-set expressions and replacing the rejected-response display with prose simplify presentation without changing the mathematical substance. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims: credential-dependent access to privileged parametric knowledge, preservation of general utility, and applicability to two scenarios. Expanded experimental support does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the random-key results as demonstrating exact-key matching without approximation and nearly impossible unauthorized bypass, a substantial new security inference beyond v1's design rationale. Section 4.4 also extends the utility interpretation to privileged-answer quality relative to SFT. The fixed-key and binary-permission limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 specifies that the additional SFT comparators use the datasets described in Sections 4.1–4.2 and documents the incorrect-key generation distribution, lengths, and counts. Existing key-placement instructions and Appendix A refusal templates are retained; substantial training hyperparameters or code-access information are not added.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for ARC-Challenge and ROUGE while removing the related-work examples on trapdoor defense by Shan (2021) and dataset watermarking by Li et al. (2020). Its central positioning against uniform safety alignment and within beneficial backdoor applications remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local changes simplify Sections 2.1 and 3.2, rename Section 4.2, separate effectiveness and utility discussion, and introduce a robustness subsection. Appendices B and C organize relocated metric definitions and the existing case study.

P2.justification: The utility bar chart in v1 Figure 4 is replaced by a substantially expanded full-width Table 1. Access-control Table 2 gains model grouping, and incorrect-key Table 3 is added. The metric table moves to Appendix B as Table 4, while Figure 3 moves to Appendix C, substantially reorganizing the empirical presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses two important gaps: single-model validation and missing quantitative evaluation of authorized answers on protected tasks. Table 1 compares answer quality with direct SFT and separates keyed from unkeyed utility across three models, substantially strengthening evidence for useful access control. These gains outweigh notable weaknesses: Section 4.5 overgeneralizes limited random-key tests into sweeping security assurances, and the limitation claiming only one backbone was evaluated remains outdated.
